item.title: Assignment 9: Reflections
item.dc:creator: pedro
item.description: This unit started many months ago. The first step was a test project: a short Portuguese carol for the school’s winter concert, written for the secondary students’ string orchestra and choir. That project was performed...
item.content:encoded:
This unit started many months ago. The first step was a test project: a short Portuguese carol for the school’s winter concert, written for the secondary students’ string orchestra and choir. That project was performed live, which I hadn’t experienced before with my own music. It also taught me something I hadn’t expected to learn so early. Despite the goodwill on all sides, the process felt more like a commission than a collaboration. I was doing the creative work and the teachers were accommodating it. I put that observation down to time pressure and assumed the main project would be different.

When the main project began, I went in hoping for genuine creative exchange. What I got instead was just some inputs. The String Orchestra Director told me to move the key from C to A, which made the strings easier to play. She simplified the string parts significantly throughout. The drama teacher who joined late corrected one Portuguese line from “Nós construímos” to “Que construímos”. Those were the moments where someone pushed back on a creative decision, and they were the exception rather than the pattern.

For the middle months of the project, I was working alone. The school was managing field trips, then holidays, then the lead-up to the end of year. By any means I felt the teachers were disengaged. They were stretched, and this project sat below everything else on the priority list. It’s the clearest thing I learned about working with schools: unless a project is treated as institutional priority, it depends entirely on the goodwill of individual teachers, and goodwill has limits. I should have anticipated that rather than discovering it midway through.

But looking on the positive side, those limitations forced completion. At the start of the unit I’d said that having people waiting for me would make me finish things, because I tend to start and drift. The school had a deadline and a real context, and because of that the piece got written: three movements, concept, lyrics, and music, all from scratch. The limitations I found frustrating creatively were the same ones that stopped me from procrastinating. That’s not a comfortable thing to admit, but it’s accurate.

Looking back, the creative exchange I was hoping to find in the collaboration was found in my tutorials with my Tutor where genuine dialogue happened. He reframed my frustration at working alone by pointing out that collaboration isn’t always working closely with people; it’s working effectively with people. That shifted how I understood what I was doing during the long stretches without school input. More creatively, the structure of Part 3 came directly from a suggestion he made: give each group a few bars, let the conductor activate and silence them. I took that idea and built the most successful section of the piece from it. The honest version of this project’s collaboration map includes my Tutor, and perhaps I should have named him as a collaborator from the start.

The practice session in June was the only time I saw the piece with real students, and it told me things the score couldn’t. Part 2 landed because I’d written it to be accessible, and watching the students pick it up quickly confirmed that the decision to keep it simple was the right one. Part 3 held their attention longer than anything else, because they never knew exactly when to come in, so they stayed alert. The drama group improvised a staging around Part 1 that I hadn’t written for, which reminded me that a score is a starting point and not a fixed thing. What struck me most, though, was a conversation with John at the end of the session. He suggested the bridge concept was strong enough to work in any school context. It was the most direct and generous feedback I received on the work across the entire unit.

Looking back at the full arc, the collaboration started as an open creative invitation, ran as a commission for most of the composition process, and opened slightly at the end. Using Taylor’s typology, it sat closest to the consultative model throughout: I generated the concept, the structure, and the music, and what came back was domain expertise and approval rather than creative input. There were moments of interactive co-operation, when Elena revised the string parts or flagged what the students could actually play, and those moments changed the music. But they didn’t change who was imagining the piece. What I’ve concluded is that this isn’t a structural failure so much as a condition I should have named earlier. I went in wanting something closer to interactive co-operation across the whole project and didn’t say so at the outset.

item.title: Exercise 2: Evaluate
item.dc:creator: pedro
item.description: The brief for this exercise asks for notes produced in a meeting with collaborators to evaluate the project together. That meeting didn’t happen as I hoped it would. By the time the school year ended,...
item.content:encoded:
The brief for this exercise asks for notes produced in a meeting with collaborators to evaluate the project together. That meeting didn’t happen as I hoped it would.

By the time the school year ended, the String Orchestra Director, Elena, Drama Director, António and Choir Coordinator, John, were already moving into summer. The project had always sat below their core responsibilities, and finding time for a structured reflection session wasn’t realistic. I’m disappointed by that, though I understand it. The absence of a formal feedback exchange was itself one of the things I found hardest about this collaboration: without a structured space to hear what the teachers thought, I was evaluating the work largely from my own perspective throughout.

What I do have is a conversation with John at the end of the practice session in June. It was informal and brief, but it was the most direct exchange I had with any collaborator about the work itself. His observation that the piece could work in any school, and his encouragement to develop it further, were the clearest pieces of feedback I received. I’ve used that conversation, alongside my own observations from the session, as the basis for the evaluation notes below.

The practice session was the first time I saw any of this live. The teachers played the Sibelius audio on speakers so the students could hear the piece as they worked through it. I started by explaining the concept and ended by telling the group I was a living composer. John mentioned afterwards that the students were intrigued by that, because they are used to working with music by people who are already dead. I told them that if they had ideas or changes they wanted to make, they could come to me and we could update the piece together.

Part 1 ran to almost seven minutes. With sixty fifth graders in the same space, attention was never going to hold the whole way through, and it didn’t. But there were moments that cut through, for example the choir shouting the dates was one of them. The drama group also improvised a staging around it, which I hadn’t anticipated and which added something the score alone couldn’t.

Part 2 was the clearest success of the three in terms of the students’ engagement with the actual music. I wrote it to be melodic and accessible, closer to a pop song, and that showed in how quickly they picked it up. They had three rehearsals, and they were already singing it well. The strings were looser, partly because it was the first year many of those students had played strings at all. Elena had simplified the string parts significantly across all three parts, which made it more achievable.

Part 3 was the one that surprised me most. The improvised structure meant the students never knew exactly when it was their turn to come in, and that kept them focused in a way that more conventional notation didn’t. Even the teachers were visibly enjoying it. That’s the part I want to develop further. The idea of structured improvisation with students that age feels like it has more life in it than anything else in the piece.

In terms of how the collaboration worked, I said in earlier assignments that it felt more like a commission than a genuine creative exchange, and I stand by that. On the test project that preceded this, I had a similar feeling but put it down to time pressure. The same dynamic repeated here, which tells me it wasn’t incidental. The teachers had a genuine willingness to go deeper into the work, but the problem was bandwidth. Between all their other responsibilities, this project kept getting pushed back, and by the time they could really focus on it, the available time was too short for the kind of creative exchange I’d been hoping for.

What we set out to achieve, we achieved. A piece for the school’s anniversary that fifth graders could learn and perform. The only thing that didn’t happen was the live performance.

The unexpected outcome was the piece itself. I didn’t know I could write a full work from scratch, concept, lyrics and music, and I wasn’t certain until it was done. After the practice, John suggested developing it further as something that could work in any school context, because the bridge concept isn’t specific to this anniversary or school.

What I learned: I should have been clearer earlier about what I wanted from the collaboration, stated it directly rather than assuming it would develop naturally. I also learned that working inside a school is genuinely difficult unless the project is treated as an institutional priority. If it isn’t, it depends entirely on the extra effort of individual teachers, and that’s unreliable for work that needs sustained attention.

In the end, I’m really proud of this. Both projects, the test and this one. I had real doubts going in, but I believe that the result doesn’t reflect those doubts.

item.title: Exercise 1: Consider the Evidence
item.dc:creator: pedro
item.description: For this project I have the following to draw on: The score and recording of the test project. The score from the big project: three parts, covering past, present and future, written for string orchestra,...
item.content:encoded:
For this project I have the following to draw on:

The score and recording of the test project.

The score from the big project: three parts, covering past, present and future, written for string orchestra, choir, piano, percussion and narrators.

The Project 8 documentation, including the programme note and forum post.

The Assignment 6 case study, where I analysed this collaboration in depth using Taylor’s framework.

The reflective diary and documentation from across the unit.

One attended practice session. The school year ended without a live performance, but I was able to attend a rehearsal during the process. That gave me direct observation of the piece with real students, which is the closest thing to a performance outcome I have.

Feedback from John, the Choir Coordinator, gathered informally during and after the practice.

item.title: Exercise 2: Documentation
item.dc:creator: pedro
item.description: Looking back at the documentation plan I wrote in Project 4, most of what I committed to is in place. The learning log has been updated at each significant stage. Email correspondence with Elena, John,...
item.content:encoded:
Looking back at the documentation plan I wrote in Project 4, most of what I committed to is in place. The learning log has been updated at each significant stage. Email correspondence with Elena, John, António has been kept and provides a detailed record of how decisions were made and who made them. Draft scores have been saved and dated throughout the process.

The main gap is direct observation of the students. The original plan assumed I would visit classes during the rehearsal period, but this did not happen until very late. I asked Elena on 28 May if I could attend a class, and she agreed immediately. She then asked the elementary principal whether I needed any permit or paperwork to visit. I am still waiting for that to be resolved. It means my record of how the students engaged with the material comes almost entirely from Elena’s reports in the email thread rather than from my own observation.

The email thread itself has turned out to be more useful documentation than I expected. It captures decisions in real time, including Elena’s revisions to the string parts, the third movement ending discussion, and António’s suggestion about the Portuguese text. These exchanges show the collaborative process more clearly than any summary I could write after the fact.

For the performance, the plan was to have it recorded on video. However, the school year ends on 25 June and it is now unlikely there will be a live performance. I am waiting for confirmation. If the performance does not go ahead, the primary documentation of the finished work will be the scores and the rehearsal process rather than a recording of the piece in front of an audience. This is an unexpected outcome, and one I will need to address in the evaluation.

Revised Project Timeline

January 2026 Initial planning phase. Pedro develops the concept and structural approach: a three-part piece built around a bridges metaphor covering past, present, and future. First discussions with Elena and John. The proposal is submitted to OCA.

February 2026 The original plan called for meetings with 5th grade students to understand their capabilities, and collaboration with Portuguese, history, and drama teachers. In practice, this phase was slower than planned. Direct contact with students did not happen. The collaboration remained primarily between Pedro, Elena, and John.

March 2026 Composition work begins. Pedro drafts the three movements. The minimalist, Glass-influenced structure of Part I takes shape. The bilingual dimension of the text is established, with Portuguese lines carrying emotional rather than translational weight.

April 2026 Composition continues. The aleatoric structure of Part III is developed, with the conductor activating each section’s 4-bar theme unpredictably. Elena begins advising on note ranges and what is feasible for 5th grade string players.

May 2026 (early) Elena revises the string parts significantly: simplifies to unison, lowers bass octaves, adds fingerings. Pedro sends revised Parts 1 and 3 on 25 May.

May 2026 (late) Elena does the first reading with her 5th graders on 28 May. Part I works well. Part II needs further simplification. Part III is manageable. High School orchestra students are enlisted to help with percussion and support the strings in Part II. Pedro asks to visit a class. Elena agrees immediately and refers the request for sign-off. Still pending.

June 2026 (early) António Andrade, the drama teacher, joins the email thread with a creative suggestion for the first time: changing “Nós construímos” to “Que construímos” in the dual-language sequence. Pedro accepts immediately. Elena sends final simplified scores. Rehearsals continue.

June 2026 (late) Performance date unconfirmed. School year ends 25 June. A live performance is now unlikely. Waiting for confirmation.

item.title: Exercise 1: Completing Your Project
item.dc:creator: pedro
item.description: The final weeks have been mostly about the score and the first readings with the students. A lot has happened in a short time. Elena has taken real ownership of the string parts. Between 19...
item.content:encoded:
The final weeks have been mostly about the score and the first readings with the students. A lot has happened in a short time.

Elena has taken real ownership of the string parts. Between 19 May and 28 May she revised them several times, simplifying to unison, lowering bass octaves, adding fingerings, and laying out parts across pages for readability. Some of these changes altered the music. I had written high Cs and As in the basses that simply do not work at this level, and she corrected them. When she reported back after the first reading with the 5th graders, the picture was mixed: the first movement worked well and the students learned staggered entrances; the second needed further simplification and she kept them in pizzicato; the third was fine.

Elena suggested treating the final section as a loop, leaving the conductor to decide whether the piece fades out or builds to a climax. I wrote back saying I liked the idea and wanted to frame it as a deliberate improvisatory choice. I have never done anything quite like this before and I am genuinely curious how it will work in performance.

The most surprising moment came on 2 June, when António Andrade sent a note about a single line in the dual-language sequence. The original read “We are the bridges / Nós construímos.” He suggested “Que construímos” instead. His explanation was careful: the first version creates two separate sentences, while the second fuses them into one thought that crosses between languages. He was right, and the change took two minutes to agree.

I have been thinking about that exchange quite a bit. It was the only moment in the whole project where someone challenged a creative decision on artistic grounds rather than practical ones. And it came from the person who was most peripheral to the process, almost at the last minute. I am not sure what to make of that yet, but it feels like something worth returning to when I write the evaluation.

I have also asked Elena if I can visit one of her classes before the performance, partly because I want to see the students working with the material, and partly because I need to document it for the university submission.

item.title: Assignment 6: Case Studies
item.dc:creator: pedro
item.description: The case study makes clear from the start that there is no standard model for collaborative practice, and it presents several distinct types. It uses Stravinsky to show how even the same artist can occupy...
item.content:encoded:
The case study makes clear from the start that there is no standard model for collaborative practice, and it presents several distinct types. It uses Stravinsky to show how even the same artist can occupy completely different positions across different projects. For The Firebird in 1910, Stravinsky was the junior party: the scenario was fixed before he arrived, and he was there to write music to fit a structure someone else had already decided. Three years later, on The Rite of Spring, he was the dominant force and Nijinsky had to work around him. At the opposite extreme, Cage and Cunningham built an entire aesthetic philosophy around deliberate non-collaboration during creation: each made their contribution entirely independently, and the two only came together at the moment of performance. Cage’s position was that each art form should support itself without needing the other. Their method was not a failure of collaboration but they genuinely believed that music and dance did not need to serve each other. For them, forcing the two art forms to connect or align would actually diminish both.

Between these extremes sits the Bernstein-Robbins relationship, which is the case study’s main example and the most analytically useful for thinking about my own work. Using Taylor’s framework from the research task, I would describe it as interactive co-operation: there was a clear division of labour (Robbins choreographed, Bernstein composed), but each party had genuine influence over the other’s decisions at the points where their tasks intersected. Bernstein could push back. Robbins could request changes. Neither had total authority over the finished work, even if Robbins held the overall vision. The Oliver Smith dimension adds a third type: Smith, the scenic designer, was simultaneously negotiating with Robbins about what the choreography needed and with the ballet company about what they would finance. His role was closer to consultation, translating between artistic ambition and institutional reality, with decisions being made above and around him.

I recognise myself more in the Firebird situation than in any of these. I came into this project as a student with some compositional training but no experience delivering work for an institution under real constraints. John and Elena had been teaching these students for years and knew what those voices and string players could actually do.

Before this project started I wrote in an earlier log entry that my feelings about collaboration were mixed, and that I thrive on independent work. I predicted that sharing ownership and having to constantly articulate my thought process would feel energy-draining. That prediction was partly right, but not in the way I expected. The part that drained energy was the waiting. Long gaps between emails, decisions that could not be made without institutional sign-off, a performance slot that was possible but not confirmed. The independence I ended up with was not the kind I wanted. I was working alone because communication had slowed, not because I had designed it that way.

This connects to what I found most striking in the Bernstein-Robbins story: the volume of their correspondence. Because both were touring, almost everything happened through letters. Bernstein sent music scene by scene, explained his decisions, and waited for a response. Robbins wrote back with requests or objections. It was slow, but it was continuous. My communication with CAISL has gaps of weeks where I was either waiting or generating material without the back-and-forth that makes iteration meaningful. Bernstein did not send the full score at once and wait for approval.

One thing the case study illuminates that I had not thought about clearly is the role of practical constraints as creative material. Robbins built the characters in Fancy Free around the specific dancers he knew he would have. A character written as a femme fatale in an early draft became more naive once casting was confirmed. The performers’ capabilities shaped the work from inside. I experienced this when Elena told me the 5th grade string students could only play A, B, C#, D, E, F#, and G, forcing me to transpose Part 3 from C minor to B minor. The constraint changed the music. And when she returned after the first reading to say Part 1 had worked but Part 2 would need simplification, that was the same principle: real information about real people making a real piece.

The social dimension of Fancy Free is something the case study handles well and that I initially underestimated in my own work. Robbins built the scenario from direct observation: he noticed that sailors in wartime New York tended to move in threes, and so there are three sailors in the ballet. The social observation preceded and shaped the artistic decision.

My piece has a similar foundation, though I reached it through concept rather than observation. The bridges metaphor is historically specific enough to resist being decorative: the school’s founding was tied to the construction of the Ponte 25 de Abril, and that origin gives the whole structure something real to stand on. But the most socially acute contribution anyone made to the project came from John and Elena, when they proposed the bilingual narration. They understood what it means for a room full of students from different language backgrounds to hear their two languages treated as equal in a single sentence. I had not fully thought that through, and the piece is better because they did.

What I expected from this collaboration was something closer to the Bernstein-Robbins dynamic: a scenario handed to me and a clear brief to respond to musically. What happened was that I wrote the concept, the structure, the narration, the drama, and the music. Part of this was my own instinct toward independent work reasserting itself under pressure. When responses were slow, I filled the gaps with production rather than waiting.

The question the case study makes me think about is whether the Robbins role is compatible with being a student. Robbins had institutional backing, a budget, collaborators with defined contracts, and recognised authority over the project. I am a student with a copywriting background who had never done such a project before. The ambiguity about my actual standing in the collaboration is where most of the difficulties came from, and the case study suggests that resolving that kind of ambiguity early, which Robbins and Bernstein did by defining their respective domains before work began, is not bureaucratic but creative. Clear roles made productive disagreement possible.

What redeemed the final weeks was António Andrade, the drama teacher, who came in late but looked at the script carefully enough to catch a syntactic distinction in the bilingual section I had not considered. He proposed changing “We are the bridges / Nós construímos” to “We are the bridges / Que construímos,” on the grounds that the first version produces two distinct statements while the second links them into one sentence expressed across two languages. He was right, and he had the Portuguese language and literature training to say precisely why. That is the closest the project came to the Bernstein dynamic: someone with genuine expertise in a specific domain pushing back on a specific choice, with a reason, from a position of real engagement. It arrived late. But it arrived, and it changed something. And it came from someone whose role had never been clearly defined at the start, which is itself something to carry forward.

item.title: Research Task 1: Collaboration in Contemporary Music
item.dc:creator: pedro
item.description: Taylor’s paper argues that “collaboration” is used so loosely in discussions of shared artistic work that it ends up describing almost nothing precisely. He draws a useful distinction between dialogic creation and the specific, different...
item.content:encoded:
Taylor’s paper argues that “collaboration” is used so loosely in discussions of shared artistic work that it ends up describing almost nothing precisely. He draws a useful distinction between dialogic creation and the specific, different thing that happens when people are actually present together, making decisions together. From that distinction he builds a typology of four working relationships: collaboration proper (shared imagination, shared decision-making), two forms of co-operation (divided tasks but mutual influence, either within a pre-agreed framework or interactively), and consultation (one party generates ideas, the other decides). He adds that the closer the language of communication is to the language of the art form itself, the more likely genuine collaboration becomes, which is why jazz musicians can collaborate in ways that composers writing notation generally cannot.

Reading this against my experience with the CAISL piece was uncomfortable in a clarifying way. I had been calling this a collaboration, and I do not think it was, not in Taylor’s sense. The bridges concept, the three-part structure, the musical arc, the full script: I generated all of it and sent it for approval. What came back was enthusiasm, content suggestions, and domain expertise. That maps cleanly onto Taylor’s consultative type, with moments of interactive co-operation when Elena revised the string parts or told me which notes the students could actually play. Those moments changed the music. But they did not change who was imagining the piece.

What strikes me most is that I am not sure the collaboration could have been anything other than consultative, given the conditions. But the deeper issue is institutional. I was engaged as the composer. That role carries assumptions that no amount of goodwill entirely dissolves. What I take from Taylor is not that I should have done this differently, but that I should have been honest about the shape of it from the start, rather than using the word collaboration as a placeholder for something I hoped might develop. Naming the relationship accurately is not a demotion of what John and Elena contributed. It is a more respectful account of what each of us actually did.

item.title: Exercise 2: Work Sharing
item.dc:creator: pedro
item.description: The piece was conceived for live performance, in CAISL’s main performance space, as part of the 70th anniversary programme. That framing still holds as the intended form, but as of writing this, the live performance...
item.content:encoded:
The piece was conceived for live performance, in CAISL’s main performance space, as part of the 70th anniversary programme. That framing still holds as the intended form, but as of writing this, the live performance is uncertain. Responses from my collaborators have slowed considerably, and the logistical decision (confirmation from the elementary division head, integration of the drama teacher, scheduling) has not fully materialised. I have chosen to continue working regardless, because the piece is worth finishing on its own terms. But this uncertainty has forced me to think differently about what “sharing the work” means.

If the work is ultimately shared only as a score, a set of demos, and a document, it becomes something closer to time-based work in the way a film is time-based: experienced through playback, imagined by a listener rather than witnessed in a space. That is a legitimate outcome, but a different one. The audience encounter I was designing, parents in a room with children performing, becomes hypothetical. I am now writing for an imagined occasion rather than a confirmed one, which changes the energy of the compositional decisions in ways I am still working through.

The beginning has been the most resolved part of the piece from early on, and remains so. The bass and piano opening (a motif that came from my daughter Sofia, who first thought it sounded “scary” and then changed her mind when I added the major piano chords) sets the tone in a way that feels right: something emerging slowly, not announced. The narration enters over this establishing the founding year.

The transitions between sections were a source of productive disagreement with myself. The move from past to present involves a shift from rhythmic, percussive texture to something more melodic and anthem-like. I have been treating it as a slow handover rather than a cut: the strings carry the energy forward while the percussion recedes. The move from present to future is still the hardest. I want it to feel like an opening, not a conclusion, but the modular structure of Part 3 (several 4-bar loops that can be layered and removed by the conductor) makes the transition compositionally tricky. A modular section needs a clear entry point

John’s (choir teacher) contributions in March were mostly about content: historical texts about the Ponte 25 de Abril, the school’s community initiatives, the bilingual dimension. Elena’s (orchestra teacher) contributions have been technical: what the string students can actually play, which notes are accessible, how to revise the arrangement to fit the players. António (drama teacher) has not yet been formally involved. I have been designing the audience encounter largely alone, working from a sense of who will be in that room if a room ever materialises.

item.title: Exercise 1: Exploring Time-based Work
item.dc:creator: pedro
item.description: Two pieces came to mind. The first was Britten’s Noye’s Fludde, because of how directly it maps onto what I am trying to do at CAISL. It is a community opera for children and amateur performers,...
item.content:encoded:
Two pieces came to mind. The first was Britten’s Noye’s Fludde, because of how directly it maps onto what I am trying to do at CAISL. It is a community opera for children and amateur performers, with professional musicians just sining some parts, built around a single narrative that everyone already knows. What struck me is how Britten uses the congregation hymn Eternal Father, Strong to Save as a structural anchor: the audience sings it, which collapses the distance between watching and participating. The piece exists in time, obviously, but it also exists in a kind of social time, the experience of a community doing something together, publicly, which cannot be repeated in exactly the same form. The staging, the costumes, the spoken word, the music: none of these could be extracted and remain meaningful on their own.

The second piece I spent time with was Christian Marclay’s The Clock (2010), a 24-hour video montage assembled from thousands of film and television clips, each featuring a visible clock or timepiece, synchronised with real time so that the time shown on screen is always the actual time. The piece was shown at the Berardo Collection in Lisbon in 2015, which I was lucky to see at the time. What makes it remarkable as a time-based work is that it refuses any conventional audience relationship. You can walk in at any moment, and the piece will have already been going for hours. You can leave before it ends. There is no beginning you are expected to have witnessed and no ending you are expected to wait for. Marclay described it as a memento mori, and I think that is accurate: the longer you watch, the more aware you become of the time you are spending watching it, which is also the time of your life. The audience’s consciousness of duration becomes part of the work itself.

Thinking about these two pieces clarified something I had been feeling but not quite articulating. Noye’s Fludde works because the audience’s role is defined in advance: they know when they are watching and when they are joining in, and the transition between those states is part of the piece. The Clock works on an entirely different principle: the audience is never anchored to a collective starting point, and the experience varies completely depending on when you arrive. What I have not yet decided, for the CAISL piece, is where our audience sits on that spectrum. Given that the audience will be largely parents and teachers of the children performing, there is a pull toward the congregational model: they will want to feel included in something, not observed from the outside.

I should be honest about one thing Noye’s Fludde also makes me feel: envy at the institutional conditions that made it possible. Britten had a community that was fully mobilised and present. The CAISL piece may end up without a live performance at all. The more I think about Britten’s piece as a model, the more I notice that what I am actually making may be something quite different: a score, a set of intentions, a proposal for something that might one day happen.

item.title: Listening to Alanis Morissette – You Oughta Know
item.dc:creator: pedro
item.description: I have been listening to this song for thirty years. I knew it was raw. I knew it was angry. But I never stopped to look at who played on it until recently, and that...
item.content:encoded:
I have been listening to this song for thirty years. I knew it was raw. I knew it was angry. But I never stopped to look at who played on it until recently, and that changed everything about how I hear it.

The lyrics are almost confrontational in their specificity. There is no attempt to disguise the target, no softening for the listener’s comfort. That directness is what made the song feel so real in 1995 and still makes it feel real now. You believe her completely. Whether it is autobiographical or not almost doesn’t matter, because it sounds like it costs her something to sing it.

But this time I was listening differently, because I had just discovered that the bass and guitar were recorded by Flea and Dave Navarro. Two musicians I love, playing on a song I already loved, and I had no idea. Flea’s bass is the thing that gives the track its body. It moves constantly, it has that low-end urgency. And Navarro’s guitar sits underneath everything, restrained, almost uncomfortable, which is exactly right for the song.

What it made me think about was how much a player’s identity can come through even when they are in service of someone else’s work. I didn’t know it was Flea. But I felt something in that bass that I couldn’t name. It turns out it was just him, being himself.
